profile.campus: East Wenatchee, Douglas County, Washington (Microsoft data center campus, Urban Industrial Way, 340.22 acres)
profile.address: 875 C Urban Industrial Way, Microsoft East Wenatchee, East Wenatchee, Douglas County, Washington, 98802
profile.reading:
This building is part of Microsoft's East Wenatchee, Douglas County, Washington data center campus on Urban Industrial Way near Pangborn Memorial Airport, where the Wenatchee World reported Microsoft owns 340.22 acres. The first building on the campus, a 241,000-square-foot facility, officially opened in late 2022 following a $408 million construction project that involved roughly 680,000 worker hours across various contractors, and Microsoft held a public grand-opening tour in late November 2022; a second building of the same size broke ground nearby in October 2022. About 50 full-time employees staff the East Wenatchee data center, a smaller headcount than the roughly 350 full-time workers Microsoft employs across its older, larger Quincy, Washington data center operations in neighboring Grant County. Data Center Dynamics separately reported Microsoft contributed toward a new 180-megawatt substation and a 2-million-gallon water reservoir in Douglas County, infrastructure the utility needed to support the growing data center load in the area, mirroring the kind of utility cost-sharing Microsoft has also taken on around its Quincy campus. The East Wenatchee facilities support Microsoft's Azure cloud and Microsoft 365 services, housing what local reporting described as tens of thousands of servers. Microsoft has not published which of the two same-sized East Wenatchee buildings this specific OSM-mapped structure corresponds to, so this registry records the shared 241,000-square-foot figure as the best available building-level estimate rather than confirming it applies uniquely to this address.

Douglas County PUD, the public utility district serving East Wenatchee, has structured its cost-sharing agreement with Microsoft around the specific 180-megawatt substation and reservoir project rather than a blanket rate increase, a model Washington PUDs have increasingly adopted for large-load customers as data center demand has grown across the Columbia Basin region that also includes Grant County's Quincy campus.

reading.body:
Microsoft does not publish power capacity, square footage, or individual facility specifications for EAT04 or any single Azure data center campus. This facility lies within Microsoft's Central Washington region, one of the company's oldest and largest hyperscale deployments dating to approximately 2007, spanning Quincy and East Wenatchee. Without disclosed watts, racks, or accelerator counts, the technical scale of this campus cannot be translated into AI training density or competitive positioning.

Washington state has 46 mapped data center facilities but only 2 operators publish individual campus power figures, totaling 60 MW across the state. EAT04 ranks third by published megawatts in Washington, a ranking that reflects the state's sparse disclosure rather than confirmed capacity. The absence of a published figure for one of Microsoft's flagship regional hubs illustrates the constraint that most hyperscale infrastructure operates outside public specification.

This campus matters to AI scaling through its position in Microsoft's aggregate renewable energy strategy and its role anchoring a decade-old regional footprint, but its relevance to grid constraints and compute availability cannot be read from published facts. Any assessment of EAT04's contribution to AI capacity requires inference from regional power demand, local utility filings, or Microsoft's global aggregate statistics, none of which disclose individual campus workload.
